title: Compliance Review Backlog: Hire, Outsource, or Use AI
summary: Review volume outpacing your compliance team? Compare hiring, outside counsel, and AI-assisted first-pass review to find the most scalable fix.
body_markdown:
Review Volume Outgrew Your Compliance Team. Now What?


Every compliance leader knows the moment. The review queue that used to clear by Friday now stretches into the following week. Marketing is asking why their campaign is stuck. Your best reviewer is working evenings, and you suspect she's updating her resume.


Review volume grows with the business, but compliance headcount rarely keeps pace. When the two drift apart, the costs pile up quietly. Launches slip. Rushed reviews lead to inconsistent standards and missed issues. Overloaded reviewers burn out and leave, which shrinks capacity just when you need more of it.


Doing nothing isn't really an option. Most teams end up weighing three choices: hire another reviewer, send overflow to outside counsel, or bring in AI-assisted first-pass review. Each has a place. But they are not equally good at solving the problem most teams actually have.


## Option 1: Hire another reviewer


This is the instinctive answer, and it has real strengths. A new hire builds expertise inside your firm, works under your standards, and stays under your control.


The catch is math. One hire adds exactly one person's capacity. If volume is growing faster than that, you're back in the same spot within a year. Experienced compliance reviewers are also scarce and expensive. Between recruiting, salary, benefits, and a ramp-up period that can run for months, the relief arrives slowly and at a high fixed cost.


Hiring makes the most sense when growth is steady and predictable, and when what you really need is more senior judgment in-house.


## Option 2: Send overflow to outside counsel


Outside counsel solves the speed problem that hiring can't. Capacity flexes with demand, and you get access to specialists when a review calls for deep legal expertise.


But hourly billing is hard to budget. A busy quarter can turn into a painful invoice, and routine reviews cost the same rate as complex ones. There's a subtler cost too. Every review sent outside builds knowledge at someone else's firm, not yours. Your team doesn't learn from those decisions, and handoffs between firms add their own delays.


Outside counsel works best for occasional spikes and for genuinely novel or high-stakes questions. It's an expensive way to handle everyday volume.


## Option 3: AI-assisted first-pass review


The third option changes the shape of the problem instead of adding a person or a vendor. AI screens every submission first. It flags potential issues, points to the relevant rules, and suggests fixes. Your reviewers then make the final call.


The difference is where the capacity lands. Instead of adding one seat, you raise the throughput of everyone on the team. Reviewers stop spending their time on routine checks and focus on the judgment calls that need them. Standards get applied the same way every time, turnaround drops, and the knowledge stays inside your firm. Costs are predictable, too, since a platform fee doesn't spike with a busy quarter.


The natural concern is control, and it's the right question to ask. In a well-designed setup, AI never approves anything on its own. Reviewers still make every decision, accountability stays with people, and each review leaves a documented trail you can show a regulator. The AI does the first read. Your team does the deciding.


## They aren't mutually exclusive


This isn't a choice between one option and the others. The strongest setups often combine all three. AI handles the first pass on every submission. Your in-house team makes the decisions and takes on the complex reviews. Outside counsel is saved for the novel, high-stakes questions where specialist expertise is worth the rate.


In that model, AI doesn't replace your next hire or your outside counsel relationship. It changes how much you need of each. You might delay a hire by a year, or cut your outside counsel spend to the reviews that truly warrant it.


## Build a business case that compares all three


Whatever direction you lean, your business case should put all three options side by side. Start by gathering a few numbers:


- Monthly review volume and how fast it's growing
- Your current average turnaround time
- The fully loaded cost of one reviewer
- What you spend each year on outside counsel for reviews
- The share of submissions that are routine versus complex
- What a delayed launch costs the business


With those figures, you can compare cost per review, time to relief, and how each option holds up as volume keeps climbing. For most teams, the answer gets clear fast.
